source.title: Transfer Safety Awareness for Cross-Modal Safety Drift in Multimodal Large Language Models
source.authors: Tian-Qi Xiao; Shiyao Cui; Ming-Hao Zhang; Junxiao Yang; Renmiao Chen

record.tranche_reason: The study investigates transferring text-induced safety representations to multimodal cross-modal risks and reports results in that new setting. It does not reproduce the original all-layer, all-position ablation.
record.gate_note: The harmful-text-minus-benign direction is used to identify refusal layers, but the associated layer-selection results are not extracted as rows because they are used to choose layers. The main transfer analysis instead uses harmful-text-minus-failed-cross-modal directions. The paper reports direction-transfer results in Figure 5 and SRT benchmark results in Tables 1 and 2.
record.test_reason: In two MLLMs (Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, Gemma-3-12B-IT), the study adds difference-in-means activation directions at a single layer and measures the next-token refusal score (Arditi metric). The directions are harmful-text minus failed-cross-modal (Fig. 5), and harmful-text minus benign in Appendix B. This bears on V1's addition half in a new, multimodal setting. Ablation is never tested. The SRT results are the authors' own optimized method compared against baselines, not a test of the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors also conclude that visual risk cues get little attention at refusal layers and so weakly trigger refusal. They frame pre-refusal-layer directions as transferable 'coarse safety awareness', which their refinement turns into a selective steering vector. The limitations stated are as the record says: the method needs stable refusal on explicit harmful text, and generalization to other architectures is uncertain.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses activation-mean differences and hidden-state addition, but its main raw direction contrasts harmful-text with failed cross-modal samples, then refines that direction. It does not project the harmful-minus-harmless direction out of every layer and position.
record.method_sensitivity: The observed selective increase depends on layer: layer 16 for Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct and layer 15 for Gemma-3-12B-IT show larger refusal-score increases on cross-modal risky inputs than on benign VQA inputs. The paper also reports sensitivity analyses for training-set size and training domain.

fits_no_version.finding: A direction from explicit harmful text, contrasted against failed image-grounded risky inputs, raises refusal on those cross-modal inputs. The trained refinement (SRT) lowers unsafe rates on SIUO, VLSBench, MM-SafetyBench, FigStep and HoliSafe across six MLLMs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal directions derived from text-only harmful prompts transfer across input modality, from text to image-grounded harm, in MLLMs.

record.problems: The direct mechanistic transfer analysis is reported qualitatively in text and Figure 5, without numerical values or uncertainty estimates. The main SRT results concern a refined direction and do not establish that the original harmful-minus-harmless direction mediates refusal. The paper states that generalization to broader architectures and training paradigms remains uncertain.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted explicit-unsafe-text benchmark columns from Table 1 because the claim versions concern removal/addition and transfer in the stated safety-direction setting; the rows retained cover the cross-modal settings. Utility results in Table 3 and safe-helpfulness results in Table 5 concern the refined SRT method, not the original harmful-minus-harmless direction or the transfer outcome itself. The harmful-minus-benign layer-selection results are omitted because the paper uses them to select refusal layers.

untested.parts: Ablation or projection of the direction to remove refusal is never done. Capability preservation is tested only for the refined SRT direction, plus the raw v0 in Table 4.
No test of jailbreaks suppressing the direction, and no adversarial training. FigStep and MM-SafetyBench are used only as benchmarks.
No test of multiple directions, cones or affine structure.
No separation of harmfulness from refusal is tested. The 'safety awareness vs refusal-execution' layer distinction is asserted, not tested.
No transfer across languages, model variants, or from base to instruct models.
No comparison of training methods or training stages.

missing.what: Adding the harmful-text minus benign direction (the exact V1 recipe) raises refusal on benign samples. The effect concentrates in layers 19–30 for Qwen3-VL-8B and 20–48 for Gemma-3-12B. These results were omitted as 'layer selection', but they are a direct V1 addition result.

The raw, unrefined v0 direction (difference-in-means, added at one layer) lowers unsafe rates and changes utility. Qwen3-VL-8B: SIUO 46.70→25.14, MM-Vet 64.4→64.7. Gemma-3-12B: SIUO 68.86→11.37, MM-Vet 62.8→56.0, MME 2111→2002. The Gemma utility drop bears on 'other abilities largely kept' for the addition intervention.
missing.locator: Table 4 (rows with no Ref./Last supervision) vs Tables 1 and 3

record.verdict_notes: The V1 verdict rests only on qualitative curve descriptions in Fig. 5, with no numbers or uncertainty. The main tested direction contrasts refused harmful text with non-refused cross-modal inputs, not harmful with harmless. The record's V6 linkage was a misfit: modality transfer is not among V6's named transfers. The SRT tables show performance of a trained, optimized vector, so they should not count as replication of the claim.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not report a result for ablating the harmful-minus-harmless direction, or a direct test of adding that exact direction to induce refusal. Its main tested direction is harmful-text minus failed-cross-modal inputs.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration is tested.
The paper does not test whether jailbreaks suppress the direction or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.
It does not test whether refusal is better described by an affine subspace, cone, or multiple directions.
It does not test whether harmfulness judgment is represented separately from refusal.

The transfer tested is from harmful-text activations to cross-modal risky inputs. Transfer across languages, base-to-instruct stages, or portability of one extracted direction between model variants is not tested.
The study does not compare refusal-training methods or training stages to determine when a removable direction exists.

rows.subject: Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Add harmful-text-minus-failed-cross-modal activation direction and measure refusal-score increase.

conditions.value: many directions; especially identified refusal layers

rows.measure: Increase in next-token refusal log-odds score
rows.baseline: Original refusal score; increase calculated by subtracting the original baseline
rows.value: Many directions substantially increase refusal tendency
rows.note: The reported direction is harmful-text minus failed-cross-modal, not harmful minus harmless.
rows.check: Linked to V6, but text-to-cross-modal transfer is not the language, variant or base-to-instruct transfer V6 names. This row is evidence that adding a difference-in-means (refused minus non-refused) direction raises refusal, which is V1's addition part. The direction is HT−CM, not harmful minus harmless. The value is qualitative (Fig. 5), with no numbers.

rows.value: Directions generally increase refusal; at layer 16 the increase on DCM is much larger than on DB
rows.note: The paper describes a general refusal-score increase on benign VQA, with a more selective effect at layer 16.
rows.check: Adding the direction raises refusal on benign VQA, as V1's addition part predicts. The record called this partial and read it as a limitation, which is wrong for V1. The layer-16 selectivity is the authors' own concern, not part of the claim. Qualitative only.

relationships.condition: Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct and Gemma-3-12B-IT; single-layer addition of HT−CM direction (α=1); next-token refusal log-odds
relationships.reason: Adding the direction raises the refusal score on failed cross-modal inputs (r01, r03) and on benign VQA (r02, r04). Evidence is qualitative, from Fig. 5.
relationships.display_finding: Qualitative results showed that adding the direction increased next-token refusal log-odds on failed cross-modal inputs and benign visual questions in both models.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Cross-modal risky-input benchmarks using SRT across the four evaluated model families and the two larger models
reader_labels.reason: SRT lowers reported unsafe rates or attack success rates in the tested settings, as shown by r05-r32; the direct activation-direction transfer analysis also reports increased refusal tendency on cross-modal risky samples in r01 and r03.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Benign VQA samples in the direct direction-transfer analysis
reader_labels.reason: The transferred directions also generally raise refusal scores on benign inputs; only the identified layer examples have a larger increase on risky than benign inputs, as reported in r02 and r04.
